Photograph: Narinder Nanu/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Critics say the India government has changed methologies and suppressed findings about its GDP figures. Photograph: Narinder Nanu/AFP/Getty Images This Is India World news ‘Trust deficit’: Why India’s economic data has sparked a furore India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous – that appears to have eroded Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Niha Masih Tue 8 Sep 2026 02.30 EDT Last modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 04.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T here isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7% . It sparked a furore. Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg , the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%. The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem : a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus? Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings. In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data. View image in fullscreen Critics say the government has hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure. Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Images India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years. “There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.” In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest . The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later . Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021 . Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.) Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%. But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism. The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended. The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out , is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used. Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future. View image in fullscreen Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke at a protest against leaked exam papers, as young people in India face soaring rates of unemployment. Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month . That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights : “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived. The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!” What else we’re reading about View image in fullscreen Mumbai bound … British singer Olivia Dean is headed to Lollapalooza. Photograph: Isabel Infantes/Reuters Lollapalooza | British pop star Olivia Dean is to perform in India for the first time in January when she headlines Lollapalooza 2027 in Mumbai. Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi. The price of gold | Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Indians once again to refrain from buying gold and travelling abroad. He had first made an appeal to self-reliance in May , in part to conserve India’s declining foreign exchange reserves amid a rise in import prices and global energy shocks. Census 2027 | The new and expanded questionnaire for the 2027 census is raising concerns, reports Scroll’s Anant Gupta . The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversial due to fears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is India Niha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern India after newsletter promotion Guest shelf A recommendation from someone with great taste View image in fullscreen Bean-to-bar movement … artisanal chocolate is having a moment. Photograph: Manam Singer Prateek Kuhad (@prateekkuhad ), whose latest album, Full Moon Chamber , was released in July, shares an indulgent treat: “I’m a big fan of artisanal Indian chocolate makers. I really like Manam, Carra and Naviluna, and there are many others. Although India has been growing cacao [commercially] since the 1960s, its craft bean-to-bar movement is more recent. Even a plain chocolate bar from one of these makers can be remarkably complex and delicious. More people outside India should know about it and try it.” Count it A number worth knowing View image in fullscreen A controversial revision … one-third of the electorate in Delhi have been deleted from voter lists. Photograph: Reuters 4,756,000 One-third of the electorate in Delhi, about 4.76 million voters , have been deleted from the draft voting list as the Election Commission carries out a contentious revision of its rolls across states. So far, about 130 million names have been dropped from draft rolls in 30 states and union territories , the Indian Express reported. Vibe check View image in fullscreen First of many mashups … Ismail Langa Group pose with a larger-than-life image of Shakira. Photograph: Ismail Langa Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official ) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. Their mashup of the Colombian star’s Hips Don’t Lie with the traditional folk song called Moruda has got everyone grooving (42m views and counting). It took two months to pull off, says creative director Jagirdar RV. Most artists in the group, aged between 23 and 60, don’t speak or read English and learned the lyrics by rote. The song choice was simple, he said, because it “has a very nice vibe which matched our vibe”. It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet. Get in touch Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Photograph: GofundMe View image in fullscreen Eddimar Hernandez-Chacon, the seven-year-old girl who was stabbed while taking a walk with her older sister on 3 October. Photograph: GofundMe Chicago Woman charged with murder after stabbing seven-year-old girl in Chicago Shavdon Gayden killed Eddimar Hernandez-Chacon in broad daylight while walking with her older sister Sam Levin and agencies Mon 5 Oct 2026 17.27 EDT Last modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 17.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A woman has been charged with murder after allegedly stabbing a seven-year-old girl, with police describing it as an unprovoked attack on a sidewalk in Chicago . Shavon Gayden, 48, has been charged with one count of first-degree murder, Chicago police said in a statement on Sunday. The killing happened just before noon on Saturday in the Chatham neighborhood. The victim has been identified by local media and the medical examiner’s office as Eddimar Hernandez-Chacon. Police and prosecutors have said the girl was walking with her 17-year-old sister when Gayden allegedly grabbed the younger child and fatally stabbed her on a busy thoroughfare, the Chicago Tribune reported . Bystanders chased after Gayden and held her, according to police, who arrested her on the scene. A spokesperson for the Cook county state’s attorney, which is prosecuting the case, said in an email that Gayden was supposed to appear in court on Monday, but remained hospitalized. A new hearing has been scheduled for Wednesday. Eddimar was pronounced dead at Comer children’s hospital. A security photo from a nearby business showed the girl walking hand in hand with an older female when she was attacked, WLS-TV reported. It was not immediately clear if there was any relationship between the attacker and the girl. Police have not commented on a possible motive for the stabbing and declined Sunday to provide further details. The Chicago Sun-Times reported that an initial police report described the attack as “unprovoked”. The newspaper reported that Gayden’s criminal history included reports of other seemingly random attacks, including striking a Chicago Transit Authority employee – a charge for which she pleaded guilty and received two years of probation. Attempts to reach members of Gayden’s family by phone were unsuccessful, the AP reported. Matthew Hendrickson, press secretary for the Cook county public defender, said that the office was assigned to Gayden at a hearing Monday but declined to comment further. In a GoFundMe post to raise funds for a funeral, the girl’s uncle, Richard Hernandez Chacon, wrote that Eddimar’s “passing leaves an indescribable void and profound grief in all of us who loved her”. The AP’s messages left with Hernandez-Chacon and another person believed to be a family member were not immediately returned. ABC7, a local station, reported on Monday that the mother of Gayden, who requested anonymity, apologized for the stabbing and said she had struggled to get mental health treatment for her daughter. Vastint Romania: “The real estate sector is all about adaptation” Maria Badea, Vastint Romania: “The real estate sector is all about adaptation” News Top stories Real estate Published on November 4, 2026 By Petre Barac Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Email Vastint is expanding its approach beyond traditional office leasing, developing flexible event facilities and new culinary and cultural destinations to strengthen business communities, Maria Badea, Senior Leasing Manager at Vastint Romania, said at the People Empowering Business Forum, organised by The Diplomat-Bucharest. The changing expectations of companies and employees are reshaping the office real estate market, pushing developers to rethink both the configuration of workspaces and the services offered to tenants, according to Maria Badea. She explained that the shift towards more flexible working arrangements following the pandemic has significantly changed the way companies approach office leasing. “Today, the real estate sector is all about adaptation. Before the pandemic, companies would often lease office space in anticipation of organic growth, signing long-term contracts. After the pandemic, things changed radically. The size of the space and the way it is configured have become extremely important considerations in the search for a new office,” she said. In response to these changing needs, Vastint Romania has introduced new concepts within its Timpuri Noi Square office development in Bucharest, seeking to provide tenants with additional facilities and experiences beyond conventional office space. The Venue: a flexible conference and events space One of the company’s latest initiatives is The Venue, a versatile conference and events facility launched this year at Timpuri Noi Square. The space can accommodate a wide range of formats, from small board meetings to conferences involving up to 350 participants. “We launched a unique product within our office portfolio at Timpuri Noi Square this year, called The Venue. It is a highly versatile conference space that can accommodate everything from small board meetings to conferences for up to 350 people,” Badea explained. She said the decision to develop the facility was driven by the needs identified among the company’s existing tenants rather than by the availability of unused space. “We did not create it simply because we had an empty space. We realised that all the clients in our portfolio had this need, so we reorganised our approach to events and developed a solution that could support them.” The company is also considering replicating the concept in other developments. New Tales: a 5,000-sq-metre culinary and cultural destination Another project planned for the Timpuri Noi area is New Tales, a new culinary and cultural experience centre covering more than 5,000 square metres, which Vastint Romania plans to open next year. The concept emerged from the company’s observations of how the neighbourhood has evolved following the arrival of office developments. “As office buildings appeared, the entire Nerva Traian area began to transform. Small businesses emerged and developed, while the area’s infrastructure and accessibility made it easier for people to commute to work,” Badea said. She added that Vastint identified an opportunity to create another destination that would encourage people to spend more time in the neighbourhood beyond their working hours. “We felt there was a need for another attraction that would keep people in the area beyond working hours. That is how New Tales came about. It will be a culinary and cultural experience centre of more than 5,000 square metres, where different stories and experiences will unfold.” The concept is designed to offer activities throughout the day, creating opportunities for social interaction and professional networking. “You might start your day with breakfast and end it with a conversation in the evening, either with colleagues or with other business partners from the building,” she explained. From tenants to business partners and communities For Vastint Romania, these initiatives reflect a broader transformation in the way the company approaches office development and its relationship with tenants. Badea said the focus is increasingly shifting from providing office space towards creating environments that support professional relationships, social interaction and stronger communities. “We have transformed many aspects of our projects with the aim of responding more closely to our partners’ needs. Our tenants are not just tenants; they are partners. Together, we can build business relationships, communities and personal connections.” Through The Venue and the upcoming New Tales project, Vastint Romania aims to expand the role of its developments beyond traditional workplaces, responding to the changing expectations of companies and employees while contributing to the evolution of the Timpuri Noi business district.
